statement: A quiz team of 3 is chosen from 5 girls and 4 boys. The team must have exactly 2 girls and 1 boy. How many different teams are possible?

choices.misconception: I chose any 3 of the 9 children and forgot the team needs exactly 2 girls and 1 boy.
I picked a first girl in 5 ways and a second girl in 4 ways, so every pair of girls was counted twice: $5 \times 4 \times 4 = 80$.
I added the 10 ways to pick the girls and the 4 ways to pick the boy instead of multiplying them.
I counted teams with 2 boys and 1 girl, $6 \times 5 = 30$, mixing up which group gives two members.

hints: Pick the girls and the boy as two separate jobs.

Count the pairs of girls, remembering that the order inside a pair does not matter. Then count the choices of boy, and combine with the multiplication principle, because every pair can go with every boy.
There are $5 \times 4 \div 2 = 10$ pairs of girls and 4 boys, and each pair can go with each boy.

solutions.reliable: Choose the two girls first. A first girl in 5 ways and a second in 4 ways gives $5 \times 4 = 20$, but each pair has been counted twice (Ana then Bea is the same pair as Bea then Ana), so there are 10 pairs. Any of the 4 boys can join any pair, so there are $10 \times 4 = 40$ teams. The transferable idea: split a selection into independent parts, count each part as an unordered choice, then multiply.

whyOnTest: Tests choosing an unordered group in parts: halving the ordered count of girl pairs, then multiplying by the choices for the boy.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
